Complex analysis

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 29k Articles: 488
Complex analysis studies functions of a complex number, especially holomorphic functions. Its distinctive feature is that a single complex derivative controls variation in every direction of the complex plane. The map f(z)=z2 gives a first picture: straight coordinate lines become curved, yet small perpendicular arrows remain perpendicular wherever f′(z)=0.
The bottom panels show displacements rather than absolute positions. Multiplication by f′(1+i)=2+2i predicts the image of each small arrow; the exact image differs by h2. The origin is exceptional because f′(0)=0. This distinction between local conformal maps and a critical point is central: complex differentiability imposes strong geometric structure, without making every holomorphic function globally one-to-one.
The remarkable next step is that holomorphic functions are determined inside a circle by their values on its boundary. Precisely, let R>0, let D={z:∣z−a∣<R}, and suppose f is a holomorphic function on an open set containing the closed disc D. Orient its boundary counterclockwise. The Cauchy integral formula states that, for every w∈D,
f(w)=2πi1​∮∣z−a∣=R​z−wf(z)​dz.
(1)
The contour integral combines boundary values with a kernel depending on the requested interior point. It is a reconstruction formula, not merely a trick for evaluating an integral. The hypothesis about the closed disc ensures that all boundary values and the contour integral are well defined. [ref]
At the centre, substituting z=a+Reiθ cancels the denominator against dz=iReiθdθ:
f(a)=2π1​∫02π​f(a+Reiθ)dθ.
(2)
Thus the centre value is the angular average of the boundary values. For the polynomial f(z)=z2, a=1+i and R=1/2, expand the boundary data as
f(a+Reiθ)=2i+(1+i)eiθ+41​e2iθ.
(3)
Both oscillating terms have zero average, leaving f(a)=2i. Away from the centre the weights change: on the unit circle,
f(w)=2π1​∫02π​1−we−iθf(eiθ)​dθ,∣w∣<1.
(4)
With f(z)=z2 and w=1/2, expanding the denominator as a geometric series leaves only its second-power term after integration, giving f(1/2)=1/4. This also explains how the Cauchy integral formula recovers an entire Taylor series from boundary data.
When a holomorphic function has isolated singularities, a different boundary calculation detects their residues. Suppose Γ is a counterclockwise simple closed contour and f is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of it and its interior except at finitely many interior isolated singularities aj​. The residue theorem gives
∮Γ​f(z)dz=2πi∑j​Res(f,aj​).
(5)
A residue is the coefficient of (z−aj​)−1 in the Laurent series. A short proof idea is to deform the contour to small circles around the isolated singularities using the Cauchy integral theorem. Integrating the Laurent series on each circle kills every power except −1. [ref]
Here is how a complex pole determines a real improper integral. Set g(z)=1/(1+z2) and use the contour consisting of the segment from −R to R, followed by the upper semicircle AR​, with R>1. Only the simple pole i lies inside, and
Res(g,i)=limz→i​(z−i)(z+i)z−i​=2i1​,∫−RR​1+x2dx​+∫AR​​g(z)dz=π.
(6)
The arc must actually disappear. On AR​, the reverse triangle inequality gives ∣1+z2∣≥R2−1, and its length is πR, so
​∫AR​​g(z)dz​≤R2−1πR​⟶0.
(7)
The real integrand is bounded by x−2 for ∣x∣≥1, so both tails converge separately. Taking the limit therefore proves the ordinary improper integral
∫−∞∞​1+x2dx​=π.
(8)
For example, at R=10 the real segment contributes 2arctan(10)≈2.942255, and the arc contributes 0.199337, below the bound 10π/99≈0.317333. The usefulness of the residue theorem is that the same strategy works for many rational functions whose real antiderivatives are cumbersome: find the enclosed poles, compute their residues, and control the connecting arc. [ref]
Historically, Cauchy's 1825 memoir on integrals with imaginary limits develops complex contour integration and its use in transforming and evaluating definite integrals. The opening sections define complex path integrals, discuss changing the path, and examine what happens near singular points. These are recognizable ancestors of the modern link between holomorphic functions, contours and residues. [ref]

Holomorphic square root (g2=f)

Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
A holomorphic square root of a nonvanishing holomorphic function f is a holomorphic function g satisfying g2=f. It exists locally. On a connected open domain it exists globally exactly when the winding number of f∘γ around zero is even for every closed path γ in the domain. Continuing a local square root once along such a path multiplies it by (−1)m, where m is that winding number. Thus the obstruction concerns parity, whereas a holomorphic logarithm needs every such winding number to be zero.
On C∖{0}, the function f(z)=z has no global holomorphic square root: its value winds once on the unit circle, and the lift shown under monodromy changes sign. In contrast, f(z)=z2 winds twice there and has global square roots g(z)=z and g(z)=−z. It still has no holomorphic logarithm on that domain. This distinguishes the two global continuation conditions.

Monodromy

Words: 405 Articles: 4
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
Monodromy records how a germ of a holomorphic function changes after analytic continuation around a closed path. The source point returns to itself, but the continued germ of a holomorphic function need not. For z(t)=eit, 0≤t≤2π, starting with holomorphic square root value 1 gives w(t)=eit/2 and hence w(2π)=−1; starting with complex logarithm value 0 gives L(t)=it and hence L(2π)=2πi. After m counterclockwise turns the values are (−1)m and 2πim. Thus monodromy exchanges the two square-root branches of a multivalued function, whereas it shifts through infinitely many logarithm branches of a multivalued function. [ref]
The three panels use the same parameter t. They show analytic continuation through local holomorphic patches, including across a chosen branch cut; repeatedly evaluating the principal logarithm would instead reset its imaginary part at the cut. Monodromy makes the obstruction to a global branch of a multivalued function visible and motivates the use of Riemann surfaces as domains on which continued values stay distinct.

Upper half-plane (complex analysis, H)

Words: 604 Articles: 1
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
The upper half-plane is the open set
H={z=x+iy∈C:y>0}.
(19)
It contains precisely the complex numbers with positive imaginary part: 1+i is inside, 1 lies on its boundary, and 1−i belongs to the lower half-plane. In the complex plane its boundary is the real line; in the Riemann sphere the boundary also includes infinity. It is a convex set, hence a simply connected domain, and the Cayley transform between the half-plane and disk makes it biholomorphic to the unit disc.
With the hyperbolic metric ds=∣dz∣/Imz, the same domain becomes the Poincaré half-plane model. Its hyperbolic geodesics are vertical lines and upper semicircles whose centres lie on the real line. Under the Cayley transform, these become arcs of circles orthogonal to the unit circle, with diameters as the straight-line cases. [ref]
Matching colours identify each hyperbolic geodesic and its image. The vertical line through zero maps to a diameter; the vertical line through one maps to an arc ending at −i and 1. A semicircle from −1 to 1 also maps to a diameter, whereas the semicircle from 0 to 2 maps to a curved arc. Their endpoints lie on the boundary, outside the domains: the endpoints are infinitely far from interior points in hyperbolic distance.
The upper half-plane is useful because its straight boundary and explicit upper half-plane automorphisms make conformal maps and hyperbolic geometry calculable. The picture explains why shortest hyperbolic geodesic routes can look curved in Euclidean coordinates; their lengths are measured with the position-dependent hyperbolic metric.
For historical context, in his letter to Klein of 22 September 1882, Poincaré constructs a quadrilateral bounded by four circles orthogonal to a fundamental circle, and studies transformations generating repeated copies. In modern language, the sides inside that circle are hyperbolic geodesics in a disk model. The letter directly exhibits the connection between transformation groups, geometry and complex functions. [ref]

T(z)=z+1,AT​=(10​11​),S(z)=−z1​,AS​=(01​−10​).

where SL2​(R) is the real special linear group of degree two. Composition of the Möbius transformations corresponds to multiplication of their matrices. [ref]

Holomorphic function (f∈O(U))

A complex-valued function f:U→C is holomorphic on an open set U when it has a complex derivative at every point of U. Requiring a derivative throughout a neighbourhood is much stronger than complex differentiability at a point. It forces locally convergent Taylor series and derivatives of every order, as follows from the Cauchy integral formula and Cauchy derivative formula.
To see the restriction in real coordinates, write z=x+iy and f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y). The real and imaginary increment quotients must agree, giving the Cauchy-Riemann equations
ux​=vy​,uy​=−vx​,f′=ux​+ivx​.
(25)
Conversely, if u,v have continuous partial derivatives on U and satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations there, then f is a holomorphic function. The equations at a lone point, without a differentiability hypothesis for the real coordinate map, are insufficient. Their role is to force the Jacobian matrix to have the special form
Df=(ux​vx​​uy​vy​​)=(pq​−qp​),f′=p+iq.
(26)
Such a matrix represents multiplication by a complex number; it has only two free real entries. [ref]
For f(z)=z2, u=x2−y2 and v=2xy, so ux​=vy​=2x and uy​=−vx​=−2y. Directly,
f(z0​+h)−f(z0​)=2z0​h+h2,f′(z0​)=2z0​.
(27)
At z0​=1+i, multiplication by 2+2i scales lengths by its modulus 22​ and rotates by its argument π/4. A horizontal increment h=0.01 gives the exact displacement 0.0201+0.02i; a vertical increment h=0.01i gives −0.0201+0.02i. The first-order predictions 0.02+0.02i and −0.02+0.02i are perpendicular, and the errors have modulus 10−4.
At every nonzero z0​, this local rotation and scaling makes z2 a local conformal map. At zero, the first-order map vanishes: reiθ becomes r2e2iθ, so the argument doubles and the origin is a critical point. Globally z and −z have the same square. Local preservation of angles therefore coexists with global folding, a useful warning when using holomorphic functions as coordinate changes.

The simplest failure is complex conjugation, f(z)=z. At every z0​ its increment quotient is h/h. For real h=t=0 it is 1, while for h=it it is −1. More generally, h=teiθ gives e−2iθ. Agreement on two axes is necessary, but does not by itself establish a limit over the whole complex plane. The Cauchy-Riemann equations need the real differentiability condition above, or a sufficient regularity condition such as continuous partial derivatives near the point. A slit joining zero and pole allows a holomorphic logarithm near the earlier compact. Approximate that logarithm by Runge theorem and multiply the rational factor by the negative exponential of the approximant. The resulting factors tend to one with summable errors on each compact. Their infinite product has the prescribed zeros and no additional zeros.

Analytic continuation

Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
An analytic continuation extends a holomorphic function beyond its original domain without changing its existing values. Formally, if U⊂V are domains and f is holomorphic on U, a holomorphic function F on V with F∣U​=f is an analytic continuation. More locally, holomorphic functions on overlapping open sets continue one another when they agree on the overlap, allowing a chain of patches along a path. The identity theorem for holomorphic functions forces agreement throughout a connected overlap once they agree on a nonempty open set in it. It also makes an extension to a fixed connected domain unique. [ref]
The geometric series illustrates why a formula can reach farther than the power series that first represents it. For z=1, its partial sum is
SN​(z)=∑n=0N​zn=1−z1−zN+1​.
(35)
When ∣z∣<1, zN+1→0, so the series converges to f(z)=1/(1−z). The rational function F(z)=1/(1−z) is holomorphic on C∖{1} and agrees there with the sum on the unit disc. It therefore continues f to every point except its simple pole at 1. In particular,
f(1/2)=2,F(2)=−1,SN​(2)=2N+1−1⟶+∞.
(36)
Thus analytic continuation gives a value at 2 without making the original geometric series converge there. Its radius of convergence remains 1: on ∣z∣≥1 the terms zn do not even tend to zero.
The pole at 1 limits the original Taylor series, although most points of its convergence circle are regular for F. Recentring at −1 gives another genuinely convergent power series,
F(z)=2−(z+1)1​=21​∑n=0∞​(2z+1​)n,∣z+1∣<2.

At z=−3/2 this yields 21​∑n≥0​(−1/4)n=2/5, even though the original powers of −3/2 grow. This is the useful idea: overlapping local descriptions can represent one holomorphic function on a larger region.
Uniqueness on a connected overlap does not imply that every path leads to the same terminal germ of a holomorphic function. Continuing a complex logarithm around 0 changes its value by 2πi, giving monodromy; the return patch can carry a different branch of a multivalued function. If two patches have a disconnected overlap, agreement on one component imposes no agreement on the others. [ref] Continuation using the rational function 1/(1−z) is single-valued: any path avoiding 1 gives the same terminal germ of a holomorphic function, even if it winds around the pole.

Entire function (f:C→C holomorphic everywhere)

Words: 2k Articles: 15
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
An entire function is a holomorphic function whose domain of a function is the whole complex plane. Its derivative exists at every z∈C. Every polynomial, the complex exponential function ez, the product zez, and the complex sine function sinz are entire functions. The Taylor series of an entire function about any finite centre converges throughout the complex plane.
The complex exponential function is a particularly revealing entire function. Writing z=x+iy, Euler's formula gives
ex+iy=ex(cosy+isiny),∣ex+iy∣=ex>0.
(43)
Thus the complex exponential function never takes the value zero. Conversely, for any w=0, choose an argument θ of w. All its preimages under the complex exponential function are
zk​=ln∣w∣+i(θ+2πk),k∈Z.
(44)
Here ln∣w∣ is the real natural logarithm, and k ranges over the integers. Substitution gives ezk​=∣w∣eiθ=w; equality of moduli and arguments shows these are all the solutions. The complex exponential function therefore has image exactly C∖{0}, with infinitely many preimages for each nonzero value.
In the pictured vertical strip −1≤x≤1, the real part sets the modulus between e−1 and e, while the imaginary part sets the argument modulo 2π. The two drawn bands each make one full turn around the same annulus; their corresponding points differ by 2πi and have identical images. Allowing all real x gives every positive modulus, so the whole complex plane covers every nonzero output.
An entire function has exceptionally strong global constraints. The Liouville theorem says that a bounded function which is also an entire function must be a constant function. Accordingly, the nonconstant entire functions above are unbounded somewhere in the complex plane, even when their restrictions to the real axis are bounded: the complex sine function satisfies sin(iy)=isinhy, growing through the hyperbolic sine. The Little Picard theorem adds a different constraint: an unbounded nonconstant entire function still cannot leave two distinct complex values out of its image. These results make entire functions useful when global bounds or restrictions on the image can establish rigidity without solving for the function explicitly.
In the opening of his 1880 memoir, Émile Picard credits Karl Weierstrass with the terminology of entire functions and describes them by everywhere-convergent power series. [ref]

Picard theorem

Words: 959 Articles: 3
Entire function OurBigBook.com
The Picard theorem has two forms concerning the image of a holomorphic function. The Little Picard theorem permits at most one omitted value for a nonconstant entire function. The Great Picard theorem is local: near an isolated essential singularity, every complex value except possibly one occurs infinitely often. The complex exponential function ez and the function e1/z show that the possible exception is necessary.
Émile Picard presented the research in 1879 and published proofs in his 1880 memoir. Its opening footnote lists communications to the Académie des Sciences on 28 April, 19 May, and 20 October 1879; sections 3 and 15 contain the global and local results respectively. [ref]
Omitted value (w∈/f(D))
Words: 58
Picard theorem OurBigBook.com
An omitted value of a function f:D→Y is a point w∈Y outside its image: the equation f(z)=w has no solution in D. Both D and Y matter. The complex exponential function on the complex plane has one omitted value in C, namely zero, and two omitted values when regarded as a map into the Riemann sphere, namely zero and infinity. Restricting D can create additional omitted values.
Little Picard theorem (#(C∖f(C))≤1)
Words: 800 Articles: 1
Picard theorem OurBigBook.com
Every nonconstant entire function takes every complex value with at most one exception. Equivalently, its image is either C or C∖{a} for one complex number a. The hypothesis of being nonconstant matters: a constant function has only one value. The Little Picard theorem guarantees existence of preimages, without requiring infinitely many preimages for each attained value. [ref]
For a nonconstant polynomial p, the fundamental theorem of algebra applied to p(z)−w supplies a preimage for every w∈C. The complex exponential function has precisely one omitted value, zero, as the explicit formula for its preimages shows. In contrast, the complex sine function has no omitted value. To solve sinz=w, set u=eiz and rearrange to the quadratic equation
u2−2iwu−1=0.
(47)
Its roots have product −1, so they are nonzero. Every such root has a preimage under the complex exponential function, giving a solution for z. Adding 2πk supplies further solutions by the periodicity of the complex sine.
The force of the Little Picard theorem is that it applies to every nonconstant entire function, without an explicit formula. The Liouville theorem already gives a dense image of a nonconstant entire function, but a dense subset could still leave out many individual points. The Little Picard theorem limits these missing points to one. In particular, establishing two omitted values proves that an entire function is constant.
For a nonconstant meromorphic function on the complex plane, the corresponding bound is two omitted values in the Riemann sphere C∪{∞}, where poles take the value infinity. [ref] For example,
m(z)=1−ez1​
(48)
omits zero and one, and has poles at 2πik for k∈Z. Every other finite value w is attained by solving ez=1−1/w. For an entire function, infinity is already an omitted value in the Riemann sphere, leaving at most one additional finite omitted value.
Proof outline: use the version of Montel's theorem for two fixed finite omitted values. [ref] It makes the rescaled holomorphic functions gn​(ζ)=f(a+nζ) a normal family on the unit disc. The fixed value gn​(0)=f(a) gives pointwise anchoring of a holomorphic normal family, hence a subsequence with a finite holomorphic function as its locally uniform convergence limit. The Cauchy integral formula bounds its derivatives at zero, whereas gn′​(0)=nf′(a). Consequently f′(a)=0; arbitrary a makes f constant.
Great Picard theorem (#{z:0<∣z−a∣<r, f(z)=w}=∞)
Words: 480
Little Picard theorem OurBigBook.com
Let f be a holomorphic function on 0<∣z−a∣<R, and suppose a is an isolated essential singularity. There is a set E⊆C with at most one element such that, for every w∈/E and every 0<r<R, the equation f(z)=w has infinitely many distinct solutions with 0<∣z−a∣<r. Thus each nonexceptional value has preimages accumulating at a in every punctured neighbourhood. The same possible exception works for all these neighbourhoods; it need not be a completely omitted value, since it could be attained only finitely often near a. [ref]
The basic example is f(z)=e1/z at a=0. It is a holomorphic function for z=0, and its Laurent series
e1/z=∑n=0∞​n!z−n​
(49)
has infinitely many nonzero negative-power terms, making zero an essential singularity. Its sole omitted value is zero. For the value one, its preimages are exactly
zk​=2πik1​=−2πki​,k∈Z∖{0}.
(50)
They satisfy e1/zk​=1 and ∣zk​∣=1/(2π∣k∣)→0. For any r>0, every integer k with ∣k∣>1/(2πr) therefore supplies a distinct solution inside 0<∣z∣<r.
The diagram displays only finitely many preimages; the formula and its limit, rather than the finite picture, establish that infinitely many occur in every punctured neighbourhood. More generally, for any w=0, choose an argument θ of w. All its preimages are
zk​=ln∣w∣+i(θ+2πk)1​,k∈Z,
(51)
with any zero denominator excluded. Such an exclusion occurs only for w=1, with exactly one excluded integer k for the chosen argument. The remaining preimages are distinct and tend to zero as ∣k∣→∞.
The isolated essential singularity hypothesis is crucial. The function f(z)=z−1 has a pole at zero; on 0<∣z∣<r its image is only {w:∣w∣>1/r}. It omits every value in the closed disc ∣w∣≤1/r, and each attained value has just one preimage. A pole therefore has entirely different local behaviour from an essential singularity.
The Casorati-Weierstrass theorem says that the image near an essential singularity is a dense subset of the complex plane. The Great Picard theorem replaces arbitrary approximation by exact attainment, and then repeats that attainment infinitely often. This is useful when a local restriction on the image can rule out an essential singularity and reduce the possibilities to a pole or a removable singularity. For a meromorphic function viewed as a holomorphic map into the Riemann sphere, the corresponding statement has at most two exceptional sphere values, including infinity in the count; it applies when the map has an isolated essential singularity, even if poles accumulate there. Picard's 1880 memoir proves the local result in section 15, treating the cases with and without accumulating poles separately. [ref]
The Great Picard theorem also explains the Little Picard theorem. For a nonconstant polynomial, every value is attained by the fundamental theorem of algebra. For an entire function which is not a polynomial, the function g(ζ)=f(1/ζ) has an essential singularity at zero: a removable singularity would force f to be constant by the Liouville theorem, and a pole would force f to be a polynomial. Applying the Great Picard theorem to g leaves at most one finite omitted value for f.

A domain is simply connected when every closed path in it can be continuously contracted to a point while remaining in the domain.
Such a domain is a simply connected space.

A crosscut of a planar domain is a simple open arc inside the domain whose two endpoints are distinct boundary points, interpreted as prime ends when necessary. In a simply connected domain it divides the domain into two components. In the half-plane, a bounded crosscut joining two real points separates the intervening real interval from infinity; a Loewner chain completing that crosscut swallows this interval.

Cauchy principal value (PV∫)

Words: 891 Articles: 1
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
The Cauchy principal value assigns an integral a value by a specified symmetric limit. Its simplest example is 1/x on [−1,1]: delete (−ε,ε), integrate what remains, and obtain zero for every ε>0. The positive signed area under a graph cancels the negative one, although each grows without bound as the gap closes. This is a useful cancellation rule, but it does not make the ordinary improper integral exist.
Precisely, let a<c<b be finite and suppose that the two truncated integrals below exist for every sufficiently small ε>0. The local Cauchy principal value at c is
PV∫ab​f(x)dx=limε↓0​(∫ac−ε​f(x)dx+∫c+εb​f(x)dx),
(60)
provided the combined limit is finite. The same ε removes equal distances on the two sides of c; the outer endpoints a,b need not be equally distant from c. By contrast, the ordinary improper integral requires both one-sided limits to be finite separately before adding them. Whenever those separate limits exist, the Cauchy principal value agrees with their sum.[ref]
For 1/x, the natural logarithm gives
∫−1−ε​xdx​=logε⟶−∞,∫ε1​xdx​=−logε⟶+∞.
(61)
Their sum is zero at every positive cutoff, so PV∫−11​dx/x=0. This calculation adds two finite truncated integrals and then takes a limit; it never assigns a meaning to −∞+∞. If the left and right deletion widths are instead ε−​ and ε+​, then
∫−1−ε−​​xdx​+∫ε+​1​xdx​=logε+​ε−​​.
(62)
Thus a ratio tending to r>0 produces logr: choosing ε−​=2ε+​ gives log2, and choosing ε−​=ε+2​ makes the sum tend to −∞. Both widths can tend to zero without selecting a unique answer. The local Cauchy principal value selects the ratio 1.
Unequal outer endpoints leave a finite contribution even with symmetric local deletion. For A,B>0,
PV∫−AB​xdx​=logAB​;PV∫−12​xdx​=log2.
(63)
More generally, for a function h with continuous derivative on [a,b], subtract its value at the possible simple pole:
PV∫ab​x−ch(x)​dx=h(c)logc−ab−c​+∫ab​x−ch(x)−h(c)​dx.
(64)
The quotient in the last integral extends continuously to h′(c) at c. This formula explains both the cancellation and a practical way to compute it: integrate a continuous remainder instead of subtracting two large, nearly equal divergent contributions.
A finite Cauchy principal value is weaker than absolute convergence. Indeed,
∫−1−ε​∣x∣dx​+∫ε1​∣x∣dx​=2log(1/ε)⟶+∞.
(65)
Taking the absolute value destroys the cancellation. Even the Cauchy principal value need not exist: 1/x2 gives 2(1/ε−1)→+∞ on the same truncated interval. Absolute integrability makes the cutoff prescription unnecessary; an ordinary improper integral can also converge without absolute convergence, as the Dirichlet integral illustrates. The three notions should therefore be checked separately.
There is an independent Cauchy principal value at infinity. For a function integrable on every finite interval, define
PV∫−∞∞​f(x)dx=limR→∞​∫−RR​f(x)dx,
(66)
when the limit is finite. The ordinary improper integral instead requires convergence of the two tails separately.[ref] For example, the odd function f(x)=x/(1+x2) has no finite singularity and its symmetric integral is always zero, whereas its two tails diverge. Unequal truncations give
∫−AB​1+x2x​dx=21​log1+A21+B2​.
(67)
Letting B/A→r>0 as A,B→∞ yields logr. Symmetry at infinity is therefore a separate choice from symmetry near a finite pole. When both are needed, state both prescriptions, for example first take the local Cauchy principal value at fixed R and then let R→∞; coupling the two cutoffs requires its own justification.
The local cancellation also defines the principal-value reciprocal distribution. Since 1/x is not a locally integrable function across zero, its action on a test function φ is prescribed by
⟨PVx1​,φ⟩=limε↓0​∫∣x∣>ε​xφ(x)​dx=∫0∞​xφ(x)−φ(−x)​dx.
(68)
The test function is smooth with compact support, so the last numerator removes the singular constant contribution: its quotient tends to 2φ′(0) at zero and vanishes sufficiently far away. This defines a distribution, not a finite pointwise value of 1/x at zero. It extends to Schwartz functions as a tempered distribution, and is also the distributional derivative of the logarithmic modulus.[ref] Using an asymmetric local cutoff ratio r>0 would add (logr)φ(0) to this action, equivalently adding (logr) times the Dirac delta function. Thus the cutoff choice matters even after passing to distributions.
Why keep this prescription? A Fourier transform naturally encounters such a kernel. With f​(k)=∫R​f(x)e−ikxdx, pairing x and −x gives, for k=0 and 0<ε<R,
∫ε<∣x∣<R​xe−ikx​dx=−2i∫εR​xsin(kx)​dx⟶−iπsgn(k).
(69)
The cosine contribution is an odd function and cancels locally; the sine contribution has a removable singularity and its tail converges by the Dirichlet integral. This is the Fourier transform of a principal-value reciprocal, with sgn the sign function. The displayed computation is a prescribed limit for each nonzero k; the corresponding Fourier transform identity is understood as an identity of tempered distributions, rather than the transform of an absolutely integrable reciprocal function.
The Hilbert transform uses exactly this principal-value reciprocal distribution as a convolution kernel. In the convention already used here,
Hf(y)=π1​PV∫R​y−xf(x)​dx,Hf​(k)=−isgn(k)f​(k)
(70)
for Schwartz functions f, with the second identity interpreted through tempered distributions. Hence the singular integral has a simple description as a Fourier multiplier.[ref] For the bounded pure tone cos(ωx) with ω>0, the same calculation with symmetric deletion about x=y and symmetric truncation of x−y at infinity gives Hcos(ωy)=sin(ωy) and Hsin(ωy)=−cos(ωy). These tones lie outside the Schwartz space; their prescribed Cauchy principal values explain the quarter-cycle shift in the figure. Both figures are calculated mathematical illustrations. Reversing the Hilbert denominator reverses these signs; NIST uses that opposite convention.[ref]

Gamma function (Γ)

Words: 1k Articles: 27
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
The Gamma function extends factorials to a continuous argument. Its defining Gamma integral is
Γ(z)=∫0∞​tz−1e−tdt,Rez>0,
(76)
where tz−1=exp((z−1)logt) uses the real natural logarithm for t>0. The Gamma function recurrence gives its meromorphic continuation to the complex plane, with simple poles at 0,−1,−2,… and no zeros. See Gamma function residue at a nonpositive integer and Gamma function has no zeros for proof outlines.[ref]
For nonnegative integers n, the factorial identity has a shift of one:
Γ(n+1)=n!,Γ(1)=1,Γ(2)=1,Γ(3)=2,Γ(4)=6.
(77)
Thus Γ(n)=(n−1)! for positive integers n. Half-integer arguments supply a different familiar constant:
Γ(21​)=π​,Γ(23​)=2π​​.
(78)
The first value follows from the Gaussian integral; the second follows from the Gamma function recurrence.[ref]
The plot shows only positive real arguments; the Gamma function also accepts complex numbers away from its poles. Matching the factorials alone does not select a unique interpolation, even if the Gamma function recurrence is imposed: f(x)=Γ(x)exp(sin(2πx)) has the same positive-integer values and the same recurrence relation. The Bohr-Mollerup theorem supplies the extra condition that selects the Gamma function.
The useful idea is to replace a discrete product of numbers by an integral whose exponent varies continuously. The Gamma integral then evaluates whole families of integrals at once, provides the normalizing constant for the Gamma distribution in probability theory, and appears in physics, for example in the Bose integral. Its large-positive-argument growth reconnects this continuous description to factorials through Stirling's formula.[ref]
Historically, Leonhard Euler studied the interpolation of factorials in his paper E19, written in 1729 and published in 1738. His integral over (0,1) becomes the Gamma integral after a change of variables, with the same one-step shift in the argument.[ref]

Meromorphic differential on a Riemann surface (ω=f(z)dz)

Words: 90
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
A meromorphic differential is specified in each holomorphic chart by a meromorphic coefficient f(z), with the coefficients transforming by the coordinate derivative so that the one-form agrees on overlaps. The derivative of a meromorphic function gives such a differential, and the ratio of two nonzero differentials is a meromorphic function. Orders of zeros and poles are independent of chart because coordinate derivatives are nonvanishing holomorphic factors. On a compact connected surface the sum of orders of a nonzero differential is 2g−2, allowing its divisor to determine the genus.

Hyperbolic Riemann surface in potential theory

Words: 88
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
A noncompact Riemann surface is hyperbolic in potential theory when its Green-function exhaustion has a finite limit, equivalently when it admits a positive Green function on a Riemann surface. This definition does not assume a disk uniformization. The unit disk is an example, since −log∣z∣ is its positive Green function with pole zero. For simply connected surfaces this is equivalent to being conformally equivalent to the disk. For general surfaces, potential-theoretic hyperbolicity should not be conflated with the condition that the universal cover is the disk: some surfaces with disk universal cover have no positive Green function.

Compact Riemann surface

Words: 44
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
A Riemann surface which is compact as a topological space. For a connected one of genus g, the Riemann-Roch theorem gives g independent holomorphic differential forms. The Riemann bilinear relations for a compact surface make their normalized periods a full lattice in Cg, and the Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface turns this lattice into a complex torus encoding divisor classes.

Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface (AJ:C(d)→H0(C,KC​)∨/H1​(C,Z))

Words: 133 Articles: 1
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
Integration of holomorphic differential forms along cycles embeds the first homology group as a full Euclidean lattice in H0(C,KC​)∨. Fixing a base point, sum the path integrals to the points of an effective complex analytic divisor. Different path choices differ by that lattice. The Abel theorem for divisors identifies the fibres with linear equivalence of divisors.

Abel theorem for divisors

Words: 92
Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface OurBigBook.com
A degree-zero complex analytic divisor E on a compact Riemann surface is principal exactly when its Abel-Jacobi map of a compact Riemann surface is zero. Normalize a differential of the third kind with residues equal to the coefficients of E. The Riemann bilinear relations for a compact surface express its b-periods as 2πi times the Abel integrals. If those integrals are in the period lattice, subtract a suitable integral multiple of the normalized holomorphic differential forms; all periods then lie in 2πiZ, so exponentiation gives the required meromorphic function. Conversely, the logarithmic differential of a meromorphic function has integer residues and periods in 2πiZ, giving a zero Abel class by the same calculation.

Differential of the third kind

Words: 74
Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
A meromorphic one-form on a compact Riemann surface with only simple poles is a differential of the third kind. Prescribed residues can be realized exactly when their sum is zero: in the residue exact sequence for KC​(S), the obstruction in H1(C,KC​)≅C is the sum of residues. Subtracting a holomorphic differential form normalizes its a-periods. Integer residues and periods in 2πiZ make the exponential of its integral a single-valued meromorphic function with those orders of zeros and poles.

Riemann surfaces OurBigBook.com
For a compact Riemann surface with a symplectic basis ai​,bi​ of its first homology group, cutting along that basis and integrating a primitive gives
∫C​ω∧η=∑i​(∫ai​​ω∫bi​​η−∫bi​​ω∫ai​​η)
(103)
for closed smooth one-forms. For a holomorphic differential form ω and a differential of the third kind η, the corresponding boundary calculation gives
∑i​(∫ai​​ω∫bi​​η−∫bi​​ω∫ai​​η)=2πi∑P​resP​(η)∫P0​P​ω.
(104)
The paths and representatives of the cycles are chosen in the same cut surface. Normalized holomorphic differential forms consequently have a symmetric period matrix with positive definite imaginary part.

For a finite group generated by A,B, glue sheets labeled by the group over the three-punctured Riemann sphere using left monodromy multiplication. Fill the punctures by the local power charts dictated by the orders m,n,r of A,B,AB. Right multiplication by inverses defines the commuting deck action. Its nontrivial stabilizers are conjugates of the corresponding cyclic subgroups. The Riemann-Hurwitz formula gives the displayed Euler characteristic. A compatible metric can be averaged over the group; in genus at least two the invariant hyperbolic metric is canonical by the uniformization theorem.

Such an isometry need not come from conjugating the subgroups inside the original deck group, so a Gassmann equivalent pair can be isometric despite nonconjugacy there.

Exhaust a simply connected hyperbolic Riemann surface in potential theory by compact bordered Jordan domains Rn​. Their Green functions on a Riemann surface Gn​(⋅,p) have logarithmic poles and zero boundary values. Exponentiating their harmonic conjugates produces proper degree-one maps fn​:Rn​→D with fn​(p)=0. If Gn​=−log∣ζ∣+cn​+o(1), normalize fn′​(p)=e−cn​>0. Domain monotonicity and a global positive Green function bound cn​ increasingly from above. Thus Montel theorem gives a nonconstant limit F, which is injective by the locally uniform limit of univalent functions theorem. The Schwarz lemma makes F′(p) extremal among normalized disk-valued maps. If F omitted a=0, taking a global holomorphic square root of a disk automorphism applied to F, then renormalizing at p, would multiply its derivative by (1+∣a∣)/(2∣a∣​)>1. Thus F is onto and gives the desired biholomorphism.

Let f:X→Y be a nonconstant holomorphic map between compact Riemann surfaces that are connected spaces, without boundary. Write gX​,gY​ for their genera and d≥1 for the degree of a holomorphic map. With analytic ramification index ep​ at each p∈X, the formula is
2gX​−2=d(2gY​−2)+∑p∈X​(ep​−1),χ(X)=dχ(Y)−∑p∈X​(ep​−1).

Here χ=2−2g is the Euler characteristic. Only finitely many ramification points contribute. The holomorphic map is automatically surjective; the valency theorem gives ∑p∈f−1(y)​ep​=d even at a branch value of a holomorphic map. Constant maps are excluded.[ref]
The useful interpretation is that total ramification of a holomorphic map measures how much the source Euler characteristic falls short of d copies of the target. The ramification of a power map of the Riemann sphere spends that entire correction at two points; the double cover of the sphere with four branch values spends it at four points and produces a genus-one surface.

Runge's theorem

Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
A holomorphic function near a compact set can be uniformly approximated by rational functions with poles in prescribed complementary components; connected complement permits polynomials.

Uniform rational approximation algebra with prescribed poles

Words: 100
Runge's theorem OurBigBook.com
Let K⊂C be compact and permit polynomial terms and finite poles in S⊂C∖K, meeting every bounded complementary component. In the uniform closure A of these rational functions, the coordinate u(z)=z has spectrum exactly K. Indeed the set of λ∈/K with (u−λ)−1∈A is relatively open by invertibility and relatively closed by uniform continuity of the scalar resolvent; it meets each component by a prescribed pole, or by a Neumann expansion at infinity. It is therefore all of C∖K. Holomorphic functional calculus then places every function holomorphic near K in A, proving prescribed-pole Runge approximation theorem.

Pointwise polynomial approximation of a half-plane sign

Words: 120
Polynomial Runge theorem OurBigBook.com
There is a sequence of complex polynomials converging pointwise on the whole plane to the sign of the imaginary part, with value zero on the real axis. For each n, take the compact union of the upper rectangle [−n,n]+i[1/n,n], its lower reflection and the real segment [−n,n]. Its complement is connected. The function equal to one, minus one and zero on disjoint neighborhoods of the three components is holomorphic. The polynomial Runge theorem provides a polynomial within 1/n of it on the union. Every fixed point lies in its corresponding component for all large n, proving pointwise convergence. The limit is discontinuous, so the convergence cannot be locally uniform near the real axis. This illustrates how pointwise approximation by holomorphic functions differs from locally uniform approximation.

Winding number (wind(γ,w))

Words: 338 Articles: 2
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
The winding number records how many net turns a closed piecewise smooth curve makes around a chosen point w. Counterclockwise turns contribute positively, clockwise turns negatively. It measures a traversal, including repeated visits; a drawing of the curve's outline alone can lose that information. For a closed curve γ avoiding w,
wind(γ,w)=2πi1​∫γ​z−wdz​.
(142)
Equivalently, continuously follow an argument of γ(t)−w along one journey and divide its total change by 2π. The start and endpoint agree as complex numbers, so the change is an integer number of full turns. The principal argument at the endpoints cannot retain those turns; a continuous choice along the parametrized path can.[ref]
For γ(t)=eit, 0≤t≤2π, the winding number about zero is one. Traversing the same unit circle twice makes it two; reversing its orientation of a contour makes it negative. The winding number about w=2 is zero: the same journey now stays to one side of the point being measured. Joining one counterclockwise loop and one clockwise loop around zero gives net winding number zero even though both loops encircle zero.
The winding number does not change during a homotopy of closed curves avoiding w. This is why it is useful: complicated curves can often be deformed to simple ones whose count is obvious. The argument principle transfers that robust geometric integer to a count of zeros of a function and poles. The example in boundary sampling can miss winding shows why finite samples of a curve need control between samples before they can certify the same winding number.

This is a local condition: a large loop around a regular point might also enclose a distant branch point, so that large loop alone cannot classify the regular point. For the complex logarithm and square root, every nonzero point has a local holomorphic branch, but a loop once around 0 changes the chosen branch. [ref]

Two turns restore the square root to 2; no nonzero number of turns restores the logarithm. This distinguishes a two-sheeted algebraic branch point from a logarithmic singularity.
A pole need not be a branch point: 1/z is unbounded near 0, yet 1/(reit)=r−1e−it returns to its starting value after one turn. Conversely, the square-root values tend to 0 at their branch point. The issue is whether a single holomorphic choice survives going around the point, rather than whether the values become large. On the Riemann sphere, infinity is also a branch point of both z​ and logz: in the local coordinate ζ=1/z, these are ζ−1/2 and −logζ, whose continuations around ζ=0 change sign and subtract 2πi, respectively. The cut can move. Choosing 0<θ<2π defines a holomorphic logarithm L+​(z)=log∣z∣+iθ on D+​=C∖[0,∞). At −1 this gives L+​(−1)=iπ and exp(L+​(−1)/2)=i, both regular values despite −1 lying on the previous cut. In the complex upper half-plane, L+​ agrees with Log; in the lower half-plane it equals Log+2πi, so the corresponding square roots have opposite signs there. The overlap D∩D+​ has two components, exactly why the identity theorem cannot force agreement between them. [ref]
For example, the limits of B+​ at −r, r>0, are ir​ from above and −ir​ from below. This jump records the chosen branch cut; each point −r=0 still has a neighbourhood supporting a holomorphic square root. Moving the cut changes the bookkeeping, while the branch point at 0 and its monodromy persist. Specifying a branch of a multivalued function is therefore essential before differentiating or performing contour integration with holomorphic square roots, complex logarithms or complex exponentiation.

Complex number (C)

Words: 2k Articles: 18
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
A complex number is z=x+iy, where x,y are real numbers and the imaginary unit satisfies i2=−1. The real part is x and the imaginary part is y: for 3+4i they are 3 and 4, respectively. Equality requires both coordinates to agree. Thus the complex plane gives each complex number a concrete position, while ordinary addition and multiplication become geometric operations.
For z=3+4i and w=1+i, addition works coordinate by coordinate, whereas multiplication uses i2=−1:
z+w=4+5i,zw=(3+4i)(1+i)=3+7i−4=−1+7i.
(150)
These answers encode different motions: addition by w is a translation, while multiplication by w is a rotation combined with a uniform change of size. Keeping these pictures distinct prevents a common beginner's confusion.
The complex numbers form a field: every nonzero z has a multiplicative inverse, computable using its complex conjugate and modulus. They also supply the missing solutions of a quadratic equation such as u2+1=0, namely u=±i. The surprising payoff is that extending arithmetic also makes Euclidean geometry easier to calculate. For a systematic introduction to these definitions, see Jeremy Orloff, MIT 18.04, topic 1, sections 1.3–1.5.

where r is its modulus and θ is an argument. The equality uses Euler's formula; sine and cosine recover the imaginary part and real part from polar coordinates. For z=3+4i, take r=5 and θ=arctan(4/3)≈0.927295 radians, so cosθ=3/5 and sinθ=4/5.
If w=seiϕ=0, then
zw=rsei(θ+ϕ),wz​=sr​ei(θ−ϕ).

Repeated multiplication now becomes especially simple: (reiθ)n=rneinθ for a positive integer n. This explains the evenly spaced arguments of the roots of a complex number. For example, (3+4i)2=−7+24i has modulus 25 and principal argument 2θ≈1.854590 radians. The Cartesian calculation and the polar form provide independent checks on both its location and its size. Choose polar form when the task concerns multiplication, division, or repeated turns; use real parts and imaginary parts for addition.

Euler's formula (eiθ=cosθ+isinθ)

Words: 228
Complex number OurBigBook.com
For a real angle θ in radians, Euler's formula states
eiθ=cosθ+isinθ,
(153)
where i is the imaginary unit. It connects the complex exponential to the sine and cosine coordinates of the unit circle. In particular, ∣eiθ∣=1, and multiplying by eiθ rotates a complex number through angle θ without changing its modulus. At θ=π/3 it gives eiπ/3=1/2+i3​/2; at θ=π, it gives eiπ=−1.
The identity makes angle addition algebraic: eiαeiβ=ei(α+β). Expanding the product and comparing real parts and imaginary parts recovers the sine addition formula and cosine addition formula. Differentiating eiωt gives iωeiωt, and differentiating again gives −ω2eiωt. Its real and imaginary coordinates therefore solve the harmonic oscillator equation. This is why complex exponentials are useful building blocks in Fourier analysis: differentiation acts on each frequency by simple multiplication.
A short justification separates the even and odd powers in the absolutely convergent power series for eiθ. The even powers give ∑n≥0​(−1)nθ2n/(2n)!=cosθ, and the odd powers give i∑n≥0​(−1)nθ2n+1/(2n+1)!=isinθ. The absolute convergence permits this regrouping. The formula thus links an analytic definition of the complex exponential to a geometric motion rather than merely introducing a convenient notation.
Leonhard Euler presents the relation between imaginary exponentials and sines and cosines in his 1748 Introductio in analysin infinitorum, volume 1, chapter VIII, section 138. His derivation uses limiting powers after connecting trigonometric addition to algebra. The original Latin and Ian Bruce's English translation can be read together in Euler, Introductio, chapter VIII, section 138.

The modulus of a complex number z=x+iy is

It extends absolute value to the complex plane: the modulus is the Euclidean distance from z to zero, or the Euclidean norm of its coordinate vector. The Pythagorean theorem gives ∣3+4i∣=5, even though its two coordinates have sizes 3 and 4. The modulus is always nonnegative, and is zero exactly at zero.
Two essential rules are
∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣,∣z+w∣≤∣z∣+∣w∣.
(155)
The second is the triangle inequality. For z=3+4i and w=1+i, the product has modulus 50​=52​≈7.071068, while the sum has modulus 41​≈6.403124<5+2​≈6.414214. The strict inequality records that the two displacement vectors point in different directions.
The Euclidean distance between two complex numbers z,w is ∣z−w∣. Consequently ∣z−w∣<ε expresses geometric closeness without treating the two coordinates separately. This makes the modulus a natural measure of error in complex analysis; the triangle inequality bounds accumulated error, while the product rule tracks how multiplication changes its size. Equal moduli do not imply equal complex numbers: 5, −5, and 3+4i all lie on the same circle around zero. The modulus records size and deliberately forgets direction; the argument supplies the missing information.

Complex number OurBigBook.com
The complex conjugate of z=x+iy is z=x−iy. It keeps the real part and negates the imaginary part. In the complex plane, this is a reflection across the horizontal axis. Thus 3+4i and its complex conjugate 3−4i have the same modulus 5, with opposite arguments modulo 2π.
The product with the complex conjugate is a nonnegative real number:
zz=x2+y2=∣z∣2,z1​=∣z∣2z​(z=0).

In our example, (3+4i)(3−4i)=25 and 1/(3+4i)=(3−4i)/25=0.12−0.16i. Its modulus is 1/5. Geometrically, taking the multiplicative inverse reverses the argument and reciprocates the modulus; the reflected direction alone is only part of the operation.
Applying the complex conjugate twice returns the starting point. Moreover, a complex number equals its own complex conjugate exactly when its imaginary part is zero. The horizontal axis is therefore characterized algebraically by z=z.
The complex conjugate also recovers the two coordinates without reading them off explicitly:

As a point crosses the negative horizontal axis, the principal argument jumps by 2π. A continuous choice on a suitable region therefore requires a branch cut; the jump belongs to the choice of representative, although the point moves smoothly.

Complex plane (C≅R2)

Complex number OurBigBook.com
The complex plane identifies the complex number x+iy with the point (x,y) in Cartesian coordinates. The horizontal coordinate is its real part, the vertical coordinate its imaginary part. Arrows from zero identify the same points with vectors. Adding 1+i moves 3+4i to 4+5i: every point undergoes the same translation.
Multiplication has a richer geometry. Multiplying by the imaginary unit sends x+iy to −y+ix, a counterclockwise quarter-turn rotation. In particular i(3+4i)=−4+3i. Multiplying by 1+i rotates through π/4 and scales every Euclidean distance by 2​. More generally, multiplication by a+ib acts through the real matrix
(xy​)⟼(ab​−ba​)(xy​).
(159)
For a+ib=0, this preserves oriented angles between nonzero displacement vectors: every direction turns equally. Its determinant is a2+b2>0, while its common scale is a2+b2​. This is the elementary geometric reason complex numbers are so useful for conformal maps.
The name Argand plane recalls Jean-Robert Argand's geometric interpretation. In his 1813 article he explicitly reports publishing his Essai in 1806; the original article is available in Argand, Annales de mathématiques, volume 4, page 133. A [ref] preserves the essay and its geometric drawings. Reading these alongside a modern complex plane reveals how directions and lengths give arithmetic a visible meaning.

Given a compact planar set K and an open neighborhood V, a finite square-grid construction gives a compact polygonal neighborhood inside V with finitely many complementary components. Remove thin polygonal corridors disjoint from K joining holes that lie in the same component of C∖K, and joining holes in its unbounded component to the exterior. Corridors can also include a prescribed point from each of finitely many specified bounded components. There remains a neighborhood whose bounded holes lie in distinct bounded components of C∖K, each containing its chosen point. Standard small polygonal rounding gives a finite union of planar surfaces with boundary. The index map from its first integral homology group to one integer per bounded hole is an isomorphism. Triangulate a surrounding disc: a one-cycle bounds a two-chain whose coefficients are constant in each complementary component. Zero hole coefficients give a filling supported inside the neighborhood; the face chain of each hole supplies a dual cycle. The cycles can be sums of boundary curves in different components. Argument principle (N−P=wind(f∘γ,0))

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Complex analysis OurBigBook.com
The argument principle turns a boundary journey into an interior count: follow the values of a meromorphic function around a contour, and count their net turns around zero. Every enclosed zero of a function contributes its multiplicity of a zero; every enclosed pole subtracts its order. There is no need to find each zero of a function separately.
Let γ be a piecewise smooth simple closed curve with positive orientation of a contour. Suppose f is a meromorphic function on an open neighborhood of the curve and its interior, with no zeros of a function or poles on γ. Then
N−P=2πi1​∮γ​f(z)f′(z)​dz=wind(f∘γ,0)​.
(167)
Here N is the sum of the zero multiplicities inside γ, and P is the sum of the orders of its enclosed poles. The image contour f∘γ may cross itself or revisit a point. Its signed winding number, rather than the number of visually bounded regions, is the quantity that counts.[ref]
For the polynomial f(z)=z3 and the unit circle γ(t)=eit, 0≤t≤2π, the image is e3it. It goes around zero three times although its drawn outline is just one circle. The interior contains one distinct zero of a function, at zero, with multiplicity of a zero three: the count is three. Reversing the orientation of a contour reverses the winding number and the sign of the contour integral.
An argument must be followed continuously along the journey. Subtracting the principal arguments at the endpoints loses whole turns: a closed image contour has the same endpoint value even when its winding number is nonzero. Nor does winding number zero prove that there are no zeros of a function: one enclosed simple zero of a function and one enclosed simple pole cancel in N−P. Known poles must be added back to recover N.
The mechanism is short. Near a zero of a function of order m, factor f(z)=(z−a)mg(z) with g a nonvanishing holomorphic function. Its logarithmic derivative is f′/f=m/(z−a)+g′/g, so its residue is m. A pole of order m gives residue −m. The residue theorem adds those contributions. Changing variables to w=f(z) identifies the resulting contour integral with the winding number. This is a local algebraic count joined to a global geometric count.[ref]
The usefulness goes beyond explicit polynomials. Rouché's theorem keeps a count unchanged when a boundary perturbation cannot push the image contour through zero. The Nyquist stability criterion applies the same counting idea to poles governing a system under feedback control.[ref]

For the concentric circle ∣z∣=r, the winding number is zero for 0<r<1/4, two for 1/4<r<1/2, one for 1/2<r<2, and two for r>2. At r=1/4 or r=2, the boundary contains a zero of a function; at r=1/2, it contains a pole. The theorem does not apply at those three radii. Moving a boundary changes the count only when it crosses an object being counted; homotopy invariance of winding number describes the unchanged count between crossings.

(169)
Multiplying the local logarithmic derivative by h changes its residue from mj​ to mj​h(aj​), or from −nk​ to −nk​h(bk​). The residue theorem then gives the identity. Choosing h=1 recovers the argument principle; choosing h(z)=z gives the sum of the enclosed zero locations minus the sum of the enclosed pole locations, both counted with zero multiplicities or pole orders.[ref]
For the rational function in argument principle for a rational function, the h(z)=z integral is 2(1/4)−(−1/2)=1. Adding the known pole location −1/2 back gives a zero-location sum of 1/2. Dividing by the zero count two gives the arithmetic mean of the enclosed zeros, with multiplicity, as 1/4. Choosing h(z)=zk similarly gives the difference between the power-sum symmetric polynomials evaluated on the enclosed zero and pole locations, repeating each location according to its multiplicity or order. These identities let boundary information constrain both the number and aggregate locations of enclosed zeros of a function.

Boundary sampling can miss winding

Words: 209
Argument principle OurBigBook.com
A finite list of function values does not determine the winding number of the intervening image contour. For example, sample γ(t)=eit only at tj​=2πj/4, j=0,1,2,3. The polynomials f(z)=z and g(z)=z5 agree at all four sampled points, because γ(tj​)4=1. Joining those values by straight segments draws the same square for both. Yet their true winding numbers are one and five, and their enclosed zero multiplicities differ by four.
Refining samples can help resolve a given example, but an asserted root count needs a bound controlling what happens between them. One sufficient certificate is to enclose the image of each boundary subarc and its interpolating segment in a convex set that excludes zero. Straight interpolation then gives a homotopy avoiding zero, so the polygon and true image contour have the same winding number. A plot that merely looks closed and avoids zero at its sampled points is not that certificate.

Elementary specialization of a hypergeometric solution OurBigBook.com
For compatible local branches near x=0,
F(2k​,−2k​;21​;sin2x)=cos(kx).
(181)
It follows by transforming the harmonic oscillator equation y′′+k2y=0 into the Gauss hypergeometric equation and selecting the solution with value one and derivative zero at the origin.

F(21+k​,21−k​;23​;sin2x)=ksinxsin(kx)​.

This is obtained from the second local hypergeometric solution at zero and its normalization.
